stories.headline: Update: Khamenei Coffin Carried Through Iraq's Holiest Shrines as Burial Set for Thursday
stories.summary:
The remains of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei were carried through two of Shia Islam's holiest shrines in Iraq on Wednesday — the mausoleums of Imam Ali in Najaf and Imam Hussein in Karbala — as funeral ceremonies entered their fifth day. Tens of thousands of mourners filled the streets, with chants of 'Death to America' and 'Death to Israel' audible as the coffin passed. Khamenei is set to be buried Thursday in Mashhad, northeastern Iran.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attended the Iraq ceremonies alongside senior Iranian officials, welcomed by Iraqi Prime Minister al-Zaidi, whose government declared Wednesday a public holiday. Pezeshkian reportedly flew home early after fresh U.S.-Iran strikes were exchanged following tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz — a significant new escalation in the conflict.

Notably absent again was Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared publicly since he was reportedly seriously wounded in the same Israeli airstrike on February 28 that killed his father. His continued absence fuels uncertainty about the stability of Iran's leadership succession at a critical moment.

The ceremonies carry symbolic weight beyond mourning: Iran has deliberately staged a grand, multi-country farewell for Khamenei to project defiance and signal to its regional allies and adversaries alike that the Islamic Republic's resistance posture remains intact despite the military losses it has sustained.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says He Will Allow Ukraine to Manufacture Patriot Interceptors; NATO Allies Remain at Odds
stories.summary:
President Trump said Wednesday he would permit Ukraine to manufacture its own Patriot missile interceptors, a significant shift in U.S. arms transfer policy that comes as Ukraine faces severe shortages of air defense munitions following a series of Russian strikes on Kyiv and other cities. Analysts and defense officials cautioned that actually building Patriot interceptors would require years of industrial ramp-up and significant technology transfer, making near-term relief unlikely.

Trump's announcement came in the wake of his appearance at the NATO summit in Ankara, where he clashed sharply with European allies over their refusal to support U.S. military operations against Iran. He reportedly criticized Spain as 'very bad' and suggested Britain's posture was 'not in the spirit of Winston Churchill,' deepening rifts within the alliance at a moment of simultaneous crises in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Supporters of the Ukraine policy shift argue it would help Kyiv build long-term self-sufficiency in air defense and reduce dependence on U.S. stockpiles. Critics, including some within NATO, question whether the announcement is operationally meaningful in the near term given the scale of investment and industrial capacity required to produce the advanced interceptors domestically.

The move comes as Senate Majority Leader John Thune confirmed he spoke by phone Monday with hospitalized Sen. Mitch McConnell in what aides described as a 'lengthy and substantive conversation' covering national security, signaling McConnell remains engaged in major policy debates even as his return to the Senate remains uncertain.

stories.headline: Former Wisconsin Judge Convicted of Obstruction for Shielding Illegal Immigrant from ICE Receives $5,000 Fine, No Prison Time
stories.summary:
Former Milwaukee County Judge Hannah Dugan was sentenced Wednesday to a $5,000 fine with no prison time after being convicted on federal felony obstruction charges for ushering a Mexican national out of her courtroom to help him evade waiting Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. U.S. District Judge Lynn Adelman, in imposing the sentence, said Dugan's conduct represented a lapse in judgment but declined to send her to prison.

Dugan addressed the court before sentencing, saying: 'I have been cast as both a scofflaw and a hero. I am neither. I am a public servant who's just trying to do my job.' Her case drew national attention when the Trump administration arrested her in spring 2026 as part of its broader effort to prosecute officials who obstruct federal immigration enforcement.

The case has become a flashpoint in the national debate over immigration enforcement and judicial conduct. Supporters of Dugan argue she was acting on humanitarian instincts to protect a vulnerable person in her courtroom and that the prosecution represented federal overreach into the judiciary. Critics, including Trump administration officials and immigration enforcement advocates, argued the case illustrated necessary accountability for officials who deliberately obstruct federal law.

The lenient sentence is likely to draw criticism from immigration hardliners who viewed the prosecution as a landmark deterrent against so-called 'sanctuary' conduct by judges and local officials. Civil liberties groups and immigration advocates, meanwhile, hailed the outcome as a sign that courts would not impose harsh punishments on officials acting on conscience in immigration matters.

stories.headline: Arizona Toddler Declared Dead After Pool Drowning Found Alive in Hospital Morgue
stories.summary:
An 18-month-old Arizona boy who was pulled from a backyard pool, transported to a hospital, and formally declared dead was discovered still alive hours later by a medical examiner's transport worker in the hospital's 'cold room,' according to a newly released police report. The incident occurred in February in Gilbert, a Phoenix suburb, but the police report detailing the events was only recently made public.

First responders performed CPR at the scene before transporting the child to Mercy Gilbert Medical Center, where a physician, Dr. Aryan Toosi, pronounced him dead at 6:20 p.m. Body camera footage obtained by a local NBC affiliate captured the doctor saying, 'If there's no objections, I'd like to call time of death.' Officers present had reportedly flagged signs of life to the physician, who responded, 'I went to medical school for a reason,' according to the police report. A transporter from the Maricopa County Medical Examiner's Office arrived approximately five hours later and found the child breathing; he was flown to another hospital, recovered, and has since been released.

Dr. Toosi's attorney, Scott Holden, said 'there is much more to this case, both factually and medically, than has been reported.' Mercy Gilbert Medical Center said it conducted a thorough internal review and has made changes to its care protocols, calling the episode 'a heartbreaking situation.' Medical records were not included in the police report, leaving key clinical questions unanswered.

Police are recommending negligence charges against the child's parents, citing a strong smell of marijuana at the home that investigators believe may have contributed to the child having unsupervised access to the pool. The Maricopa County Attorney's Office has not yet announced whether it will pursue charges against the parents or the physician.

stories.headline: IMF Cuts Global Growth Forecast to 3% for 2026, Citing Iran War Energy Shock
stories.summary:
The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday downgraded its outlook for world economic growth to 3% in 2026, down from 3.5% last year and from its April forecast of 3.1%, citing the energy shock triggered by the U.S.-Iran conflict. The IMF projects oil prices will rise nearly 32% this year and global consumer inflation will reach 4.7%, reversing two years of progress against price pressures. The fund expects a partial rebound to 3.4% growth in 2027, contingent on the Strait of Hormuz reopening later this month — an assumption complicated by President Trump's declaration Wednesday that a ceasefire with Iran is over.

The United States is forecast to grow 2.3% in 2026, buoyed by the 2025 tax cuts, AI-driven productivity gains, and a strong stock market. Eurozone nations, hammered by higher energy prices, are collectively expected to grow just 0.9%, down from 1.4% in 2025. China is projected to expand 4.6%, slightly above April's forecast, supported by public works spending and high-tech manufacturing despite property market headwinds.

IMF Deputy Research Director Petya Koeva Brooks told reporters that 'the world economy has weathered the shock from the war better than feared,' crediting existing oil stockpiles and increased production by non-Persian Gulf exporters for limiting the damage. The fund's forecasts carry significant uncertainty given the fluid state of U.S.-Iran hostilities and the unresolved status of Hormuz shipping lanes, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and natural gas trade passes.

stories.headline: Lawyer Says Detained Gaza Doctor Was Severely Beaten in Israeli Prison, Fears for His Life
stories.summary:
The attorney for Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza who has been held by Israeli authorities without charge for more than 18 months, told the BBC on Wednesday that his client had been so severely beaten during a prison visit last week that he could barely be recognized. Lawyer Nasser Odeh said bruises covered Abu Safiya's face, neck, and ears, and that the doctor told him he feared he would not survive. 'I think someone has decided to kill me,' Odeh quoted his client as saying.

The Israel Prison Service rejected the account as false. Israeli authorities maintain Abu Safiya was detained on suspicion of involvement in terrorist activities and for holding a colonel-level rank in Hamas's health ministry, which provided medical care to security personnel. International aid groups and medical staff who worked with him deny that he cooperated with Hamas in a military capacity.

Israel's Supreme Court has ordered the government to respond by Tuesday to a petition seeking the release of Abu Safiya and 13 other Palestinian doctors held without charge. Abu Safiya was detained in December 2024 when Israeli forces evacuated Kamal Adwan Hospital, which the military described as a Hamas stronghold. The World Health Organization had at the time called for an end to attacks on medical facilities in Gaza.

stories.headline: Two Girls Seriously Injured in Knife Attack at German School; Teen Suspect Arrested
stories.summary:
Two 13-year-old girls were seriously injured Wednesday at the Welfen-Gymnasium secondary school in Schongau, a small town in Upper Bavaria, Germany, after an attack by a 16-year-old suspect who was subsequently arrested. Police said the suspect was found carrying both a knife and a firearm and was believed to have acted alone. Neither victim's injuries were described as life-threatening, though Bavaria's interior minister said he believed the girls had been stabbed.

Authorities launched a major operation at the school and described the incident as a 'rampage.' The suspect's identity was not released, and it remained unclear whether the individual had a direct connection to the school. Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the suspect had previously received psychiatric treatment and that there were unconfirmed indications the attacker was a former student.

A family and parent contact point was established at a local fire station. The attack is the latest in a series of school violence incidents across Europe and is likely to intensify debates in Germany over school security and mental health intervention policies.

stories.headline: Trump Administration Clears OpenAI's GPT-5.6 for Public Release
stories.summary:
The Trump administration has approved a broad public launch of OpenAI's advanced GPT-5.6 model series, ending a government-requested delay. OpenAI announced late Tuesday that its flagship model "Sol," along with lower-tier models "Terra" and "Luna," will be released publicly on Thursday. CEO Sam Altman posted "happy building" on social media following the announcement.

The clearance marks a notable moment in the evolving relationship between the federal government and leading artificial intelligence companies, with access to powerful AI models now being negotiated on a case-by-case basis in real time. The administration had previously asked OpenAI to hold off on the rollout, though the specific reasons for the delay were not disclosed publicly.

The episode underscores the degree to which Washington is now directly involved in decisions about when and how frontier AI systems reach the public. GPT-5.6 represents OpenAI's most capable model to date, and its release is expected to intensify competition across the AI industry.

stories.headline: NATO Allies Announce $50 Billion Long-Range Missile Program at Ankara Summit
stories.summary:
Twelve NATO member countries, led by the United Kingdom, have unveiled a £37 billion ($50 billion) joint program to develop a new long-range precision strike missile capable of hitting targets up to 1,250 miles away. The Deep Precision Strike initiative was announced Wednesday at the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, and is intended to strengthen European defense capabilities over the next decade.

British Prime Minister Keir Starmer convened allied leaders to launch the program, describing it as a signal of a "stronger, more European NATO." Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper said the capability would allow allies to strike "high value military targets and the logistical engines that drive armies," serving as a deterrent against Russian aggression. NATO has scrambled fighter jets to intercept Russian aircraft more than 700 times in recent months, according to the UK government.

The announcement comes amid pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, who has demanded NATO members increase defense spending and has ordered a review of the U.S. military presence in Europe. Starmer is expected to face criticism at the summit for not yet committing to a plan to reach the 3.5% of GDP defense spending target agreed by most allies. The missile system is not expected to be operational until the 2030s.

stories.headline: German Palliative Care Doctor Sentenced to Life for Murdering 15 Patients
stories.summary:
A Berlin court on Wednesday sentenced a 41-year-old palliative care physician, identified as Johannes M. under German privacy rules, to life imprisonment for the murders of 15 patients between September 2021 and July 2024. Victims ranged in age from 25 to 94; all were critically ill but not facing imminent death. The court found the doctor administered lethal combinations of medications during home visits without patient consent and in several cases set fires to conceal the crimes.

The defendant remained largely silent throughout the year-long trial before confessing last month to killing twelve patients, claiming he believed he was sparing them suffering. The court also ordered preventive detention following his prison sentence and imposed a lifetime ban on practicing medicine. Relatives of victims testified that their loved ones had expressed a desire to live.

Prosecutors are now investigating 76 additional cases involving the same doctor. German media report that if convictions follow in those cases, it could rank as one of the worst instances of serial murder in German history. The court's preventive detention order reflects authorities' assessment that he remains a continuing danger.

stories.headline: Obamacare Premiums Projected to Rise 14% for Second Straight Year
stories.summary:
A new analysis of initial insurer filings by KFF finds that Affordable Care Act marketplace premiums are set to rise by a median of 14% in 2027, which would mark the second consecutive year of double-digit increases in the individual market. The projected hike would leave millions of Americans facing thousands of dollars more in annual coverage costs, deepening what analysts describe as a health affordability crisis.

Insurers attribute the increases primarily to rising costs for health care services and the expiration of enhanced federal subsidies that had helped hold premiums down in recent years. The subsidy enhancements, first enacted during the COVID-19 pandemic, have not been renewed by Congress, removing a key financial buffer for lower- and middle-income enrollees.

The premium surge is politically charged: Democrats argue the increases reflect the consequences of Republican-led decisions not to extend subsidy enhancements and broader ACA undermining, while insurers and some conservative analysts point to underlying health care cost inflation and structural market dynamics as the root cause. Final premium rates will be set later this year before open enrollment begins.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Declares Iran Ceasefire 'Over' After U.S. Strikes 80 Targets; Supreme Court Upholds Birthright Citizenship
stories.summary:
President Trump declared the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding effectively dead on Wednesday, saying "to me, I think it's over" after the U.S. military struck more than 80 Iranian targets overnight — including missile, drone, and port facilities — in retaliation for Iranian attacks on three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Trump, speaking at the NATO summit in Ankara, called Iranian leadership "scum" and said negotiations were "a waste of time," while oil prices surged more than 5% on news that the U.S. had also revoked a sanctions waiver allowing Iranian oil sales. Iran threatened a "crushing response" and said it had already struck U.S. military sites in the Gulf.

The escalation marks a sharp reversal from the ceasefire Trump had described weeks ago as Iran's "unconditional surrender." Both sides have accused each other of violating the memorandum of understanding. The exchange of fire risks plunging the two countries into a renewed cycle of retaliation and threatens global energy supplies flowing through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for world oil markets.

Separately, the U.S. Supreme Court issued its most consequential ruling of the term on the same day, striking down Trump's executive order seeking to end birthright citizenship and upholding the longstanding constitutional guarantee. The 6-3 conservative court's decision was a major defeat for the administration's immigration agenda, though Trump immediately signaled he would pursue legislative alternatives, creating new headaches for congressional Republican leaders.

The court also ruled that states may ban transgender athletes from competing in female school and college sports, finding that such restrictions do not violate Title IX — a ruling cheered by Republican-led states and criticized by civil rights advocates as discriminatory. The twin decisions capped a high-stakes Supreme Court term with sweeping implications for immigration law, civil rights, and the limits of executive power.

stories.headline: Update: Succession Battle Underway in Maine as Democrats Pressure Platner to Exit Senate Race
stories.summary:
Maine Democratic Senate nominee Graham Platner has not withdrawn from the race despite mounting calls from prominent party figures, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Senators Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, and dozens of others, who have urged him to step aside following a rape allegation from a former girlfriend. Platner denies all allegations, but a second woman has also accused him of removing condoms during sex without her consent, according to The Washington Post. The Maine Democratic Party's executive director said Tuesday that the party is developing a replacement process but will not disclose details until Platner formally withdraws.

The stakes are high: Maine was considered Democrats' best opportunity to flip a Senate seat and potentially regain the majority. Platner has until July 13 to withdraw and allow the state party to select a replacement nominee to face incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins. Multiple potential replacements have already begun positioning themselves, and Republicans have reportedly prepared $8 million in negative ads ready to deploy against whoever emerges as a new Democratic candidate.

The Maine Democratic Party executive director said Platner's campaign has repeatedly attempted to influence the replacement process, a claim the campaign disputes. Democrats nationally are scrambling to manage the fallout, with the episode exposing tensions over vetting and candidate selection within the party just four months before Election Day.

The situation presents a stark contrast in how each party is responding: Republicans are already preparing to capitalize, while Democrats remain divided over the pace and process of replacing their nominee. Platner, who won the primary in June, has called the rape allegation "categorically false" and says thousands of Maine voters who supported him deserve a voice in what comes next.

stories.headline: Typhoon Maysak Kills 17, Displaces Tens of Thousands Across Southern China
stories.summary:
Typhoon Maysak swept through China's southern Guangxi province over the weekend and into Monday, causing rivers to overflow, dam walls to break, and flooding that has inundated the regional capital Nanning and surrounding villages. At least 17 people have died, hundreds more have been injured, and roughly 90,000 people are affected, with state media reporting that 60,000 have been evacuated. Residents described floodwaters rising from knee height to submerging entire first floors within hours, with many families trapped on rooftops and cut off from communication.

The typhoon also triggered thunderstorms and rare tornadoes hundreds of kilometers away in Hubei province, compounding the death toll. President Xi Jinping has ordered "all-out" rescue and relief operations, but local residents told the BBC that too few rescue personnel and inadequate equipment have left thousands stranded, including a four-month-old infant without milk for more than a day.

Authorities in Nanning warned that continued heavy rain could hamper ongoing rescue efforts. A second powerful storm, Super Typhoon Bavi, is now churning across the Pacific and is forecast to strike China's eastern coast later this week, raising the prospect of additional catastrophic flooding before the current disaster is resolved.

stories.headline: Hungary's New Government Suspends State Broadcaster News Programs, Ends Orban-Era Propaganda
stories.summary:
Hungary's main public television channel M1 halted its news broadcasts Tuesday and state radio station Kossuth was suspended entirely, as Prime Minister Péter Magyar's new government moved to dismantle what it described as years of government propaganda under ousted former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. M1 displayed a message on screen reading: "Public media should not lie. We are sorry for doing it for so long," and pledged to relaunch with an independent editorial team. Magyar called the day "historic" and said it marked "the end of propaganda broadcasts on public media platforms."

Orbán, who was removed from power in April after 16 years, condemned the move on Facebook as "Tisza party tyranny" — referring to Magyar's ruling party — and directed supporters to watch Fidesz-affiliated Hir TV instead. Magyar had promised sweeping media reform during his campaign, saying a majority of Hungarian media had been captured by Orbán allies who blocked him from appearing on state television for years.

The suspension of Hungary's flagship public broadcaster represents one of the most visible steps yet in Magyar's "regime change" agenda and carries significance for the European Union, which had long criticized Orbán's media controls. The EU previously unlocked €16.4 billion in frozen funds after Magyar's election, citing Hungary's democratic trajectory.
